title: Why US Fatal Injury Rates Stayed Flat While Recordable Injuries Fell 28%, and Where Lockout/Tagout Fits
summary: Fatal injury rates barely moved as recordables fell 28%. Find the guarding and lockout/tagout fixes sitting in your maintenance backlog and get them scheduled.
body_markdown:
## **Why US Fatal Injury Rates Stayed Flat While Recordable Injuries Fell 28%, and Where Lockout/Tagout Fits**


When a close call comes down to something physical, like a worn interlock or an unguarded pinch point, the fix becomes a maintenance job that competes for wrench time with the rest of the backlog.


In plants where safety and maintenance run separate systems, the EHS lead writes up the near miss and assigns a fix in the safety system. Someone then retypes it into the CMMS as a work request or emails it to the planner, and whoever sorts the maintenance queue sets its priority, often without knowing what happened. Once the job is done, the safety record may still show it open, or it closes with a blank where the tech’s notes should be. The operator who reported the close call is left waiting for an answer, which makes the next report less likely.


Each handoff gives the fix another place to sit while the hazard stays on the floor. The delay also slips past both teams’ metrics, since maintenance tracks schedule compliance and backlog age and no field marks a job as a safety fix. That slow lane for safety work helps explain a gap that has held in federal injury data for a decade.


### **Recordable injury rates fell 28% from 2014 to 2024 while fatal injury rates held steady**


From 2014 to 2024, the rate of recordable injuries at US private employers fell from 3.2 to 2.3 cases per 100 full-time workers, a drop of about 28% ([BLS, Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses, 2014 and 2024 data](https://data.bls.gov/timeseries/ISU00000000031100) ). Over the same ten years, the rate of workers killed on the job barely changed, going from 3.43 to 3.3 per 100,000 full-time workers ([BLS, Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2014 data](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cfoi_12162016.htm) ;[2024 data](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cfoi.nr0.htm) ). The two counts cover slightly different groups, since the fatality census also includes government workers and the self-employed, and deaths have come down some since 2022 **\[SOURCE NEEDED: 2022 CFOI rate\]** .


Plants have gotten much better at preventing strains, cuts, and minor falls, while the accidents that kill people or leave them permanently disabled have come down far more slowly. A falling TRIR leads a lot of operations leaders to assume the plant is safer across the board, even as the fixes most likely to prevent a death, like a broken guard or a lockout point that won’t hold, wait in the maintenance backlog. How long those fixes stay open, and whether maintenance can even tell which jobs they are, says more about serious-injury risk than TRIR does.


A worker who loses fingers or a hand to an unguarded machine lives with that injury long after the investigation closes, and so does the family at home. Under OSHA rules, an amputation has to be reported within 24 hours ([29 CFR 1904.39](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1904/1904.39) ), and a report like that often brings an inspector to the plant. The machine involved may stay down while the investigation runs, and the crew loses an experienced person who may never return to the same job.


A guarding or lockout fix belongs in the same priority tier as a failing bearing on the line’s bottleneck asset, with an owner and a due date. Each corrective action from a near miss or inspection gets flagged as a safety job in the maintenance system, and the age of those open jobs goes on the monthly report beside TRIR, so an old safety work order on a machine locked out weekly reaches the plant manager before the next safety meeting does.


### **Why serious injuries have fallen more slowly than recordables**


Serious injuries have fallen more slowly because their warning signs usually arrive as close calls, and close calls stay off the injury log.


When a plant logs dozens of strains a year, the safety team can see which line or shift they come from and act on it. Serious accidents are rare at any one plant, so their warning signs look different, like a machine that cycled while someone was clearing a jam or a line that still had pressure in it after it was supposed to be shut off.


OSHA’s recordkeeping rule leaves a close call with no injury off the 300 log.


That makes the near-miss report the best record of where the next serious accident could come from, and at a lot of plants it lives on a paper form or in a separate spreadsheet outside maintenance’s view.


### **Lockout/tagout ties serious-injury risk directly to maintenance work**


Lockout/tagout covers the moments when someone services or repairs a machine that could start up or release stored energy, and OSHA estimates that following the rule prevents about 120 deaths and 50,000 injuries a year ([OSHA, Lockout/Tagout fact sheet](https://www.osha.gov/OshDoc/data_General_Facts/factsheet-lockout-tagout.pdf) ) **\[STAT AGE: fact sheet is ~2002 and the estimate predates it; confirm or replace\]** .


The workers OSHA lists as most at risk include craft workers and machine operators, which at most plants means the maintenance crew and the people running the line beside them. Lockout/tagout also ranks near the top of OSHA’s most-cited standards ([Safety+Health, September 2026](https://www.safetyandhealthmagazine.com/fall-protection-remains-atop-oshas-annual-top-10-list-of-most-frequently-cited-standards/) ).


Under 29 CFR 1910.147, machines covered by the standard need a written lockout procedure, and an authorized employee has to inspect each procedure at least once a year. Workers also need retraining whenever equipment or procedures change in a way that adds a new hazard. OSHA’s[amputations emphasis program for manufacturing](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/enforcement/directives/CPL-03-00-027.pdf) , updated in 2025, sends inspectors into plants to check exactly these records.


The job that calls for a lock usually starts as a work order or a PM. Yet at a lot of plants, the procedure sits in a binder by the machine while the annual inspections and training sign-offs live in a safety spreadsheet.


That split gets dangerous when a machine changes. A tech who adds a pneumatic line or a second motor closes the work order in the CMMS, and the binder procedure stays as it was, now missing an energy source. The next person to lock out that machine follows steps written for an older version of it. An inspection exposes the split too, because a skipped annual review or an out-of-date procedure is a citable violation on its own, regardless of injuries. The records that would answer the citation sit in two systems someone has to reconcile by hand.


Internal audits look for a procedure in the binder and a signature on the annual review, so a program can pass them with a tech still exposed on the machine that changed last quarter. The leaders who own that program usually learn the procedure was wrong after someone is hurt, when they are explaining to an inspector a gap their own maintenance records showed the day the work order closed.


### **Turning safety fixes into work orders gives both teams the same record**


A safety fix that becomes a work order in the system maintenance already uses goes into the queue with the other jobs on that machine, and the safety record closes when the tech closes the work order.


Set up as a PM, the yearly lockout procedure inspection lands on the schedule planners already work from. Safety events show up in the machine’s history next to breakdowns, so if one machine keeps needing jams cleared by hand, a reliability engineer can see it in both places. Equipment changes that call for lockout retraining get logged as well, since a new guard or drive goes in through a work order with a date and an asset attached. And because open safety jobs sit in the regular backlog, their age is easy to pull when the monthly report comes due.


[UpKeep Safety](https://upkeep.com/product/safety/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=Nov2026LearnSafetyBlog&utm_content=) runs on this model inside[UpKeep’s CMMS](https://upkeep.com/product/cmms-software/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=Nov2026LearnSafetyBlog&utm_content=) , where a corrective action from a safety event becomes a work order with one click. It gets assigned and prioritized alongside the rest of the maintenance work, and the safety team can read the tech’s notes once it closes.


Plants that run safety fixes this way hear about serious-injury risk early enough to act on it. With an overdue guarding or lockout job on the same monthly page as the recordable rate, a plant manager can push it up the schedule while the person it would have hurt is still working the line. Those plants also walk into an inspection able to show, machine by machine, when each hazard was found and fixed, and they lose less production to lines shut down for injury investigations.
